playbooks.playbook:
Update this enablement about {COMPETITOR} so it is true again, changing only what the evidence requires.

Asset: {ASSET}
Change that prompted it: {CHANGE}

Use the LMTY MCP tools (`https://mcp.lmty.com/mcp`), signed in to my LMTY account. Call search_profiles for {COMPETITOR} before list_products. A sign-in request is not a lost connection: say once that this needs my account, and stop. I have pasted the asset, so field questions and whether reps open it were not checked: say so in one line. If the asset carries no last-updated date, ask me for it; if I do not know, read back 90 days and say so.

1. Call list_products and list_competitors to resolve {COMPETITOR}. Pull the claims out of the asset as short statements, one per claim.
2. Call get_report_changes with since at the asset's last-updated date and limit 50, then the next page while nextCursor is not null, and keep the entries about {COMPETITOR}; then get_market_feed with family "event" and its competitorId. Several entries about one move are one change. Say how far back you read.
3. For what is true now: get_freshness for its as-of date, get_report one section at a time, get_evidence for proof and dates. For a price, plan, certification or customer line: search_profiles, confirm by website, then get_profile (overview for plans on sale, pricing for the price history with before-and-after values).
4. Class each claim current | stale | unsupported | incomplete, with why. Stale needs the change that staled it. Claims about our own product are "not checked" unless I pasted approved proof. One that my approved proof denies is unsupported, with the reason "denied by the approved claims" first, and gets no new line, not even "once approved...".
5. Order the lines by what it would cost a rep to say the old one to a buyer today. Say the order is your judgment.
6. For each line to change: Was | Now | Proof | Date, and how it is known. The change's own date only where an event's atBasis is occurred, or the price history or announcement states it; "reported on" for a published date; "LMTY recorded it on" for a report change. Where a new line reverses an old one, add a history note that never says "on [date] they did" from a recorded date.
7. List what stays unchanged (up to ten lines). If no claim is touched, say so in one sentence and stop.

Start with: changes read back to [date], [n] entries; [n] claims in the asset.

Rules: A new line says no more than its evidence. A plan, logo or page no longer shown is "no longer listed as of [date]", never "removed", "dropped" or "churned". Nothing from memory: a figure or date comes only from a tool result, my material or a page read now; a page read outside LMTY is marked as your own reading with link and date read, never replaces what LMTY holds, and never alone carries a line a rep will say. What a competitor says about itself is worded as their statement, with page and date. If a line I want cannot be supported, give the supportable version; do not soften it into a vaguer claim. Posts count as what posts say, never as what customers do.

playbooks.title: Executive Market Brief
playbooks.when: Quarterly, for the leadership review or board meeting it prepares, and on demand before any other meeting or decision. A repeat run should lead with the decision questions that are new or have changed since the last brief.
playbooks.summary: Prepare leadership for a meeting with the few competitor moves that matter, the risks and openings, and the questions to decide.
playbooks.delivers: A one-page brief - three moves with dates and sources, why each may matter, up to three risks and openings, what is not worth reacting to yet, and the questions for leadership.

inputs.name: MEETING
inputs.description: Who the brief is for and what the meeting will decide
inputs.example: Q4 board meeting, deciding next year's pricing and launch plan

inputs.name: PRIORITIES
inputs.description: Your company's current priorities, pasted in. Without them the brief asks questions instead of linking moves to your plans
inputs.example: Move upmarket to 500+ seat accounts; ship the AI assistant in Q1

inputs.name: PERIOD
inputs.description: The period to cover, if not the last 90 days

inputs.name: PRODUCT
inputs.description: Your product, if your LMTY account has more than one

examples: Prepare the competitive section for our QBR.
I have a board meeting Friday. What market changes could blindside me?
Brief the CPO on what changed this quarter and the roadmap questions it raises.
Turn this month's LMTY activity into a CEO-ready one-pager.
What should leadership discuss based on the last 90 days of competitor movement?
Give the CRO the three competitor moves that matter for next quarter's plan.
playbooks.playbook:
Prepare an executive market brief for {MEETING}. Our priorities: {PRIORITIES}. Period: {PERIOD}. Product: {PRODUCT}. A blank period is the last 90 days; a blank product is the one on my account.

What this prompt cannot do: it cannot see our deals, calls or roadmap. It links market moves to the priorities pasted above and nothing else. With no priorities pasted, say so in the first line, and write decision questions, not recommendations.

Use the LMTY MCP tools (`https://mcp.lmty.com/mcp`), signed in to my account. A sign-in request is not a lost connection: say once that this needs my account, and stop.

1. Call list_products, then list_competitors and get_freshness. With several products and none named, list them in one line and stop.
2. Call get_report_changes with since at the period start and limit 50, then the next page while nextCursor is not null; skip `created` entries. Call get_market_feed with family "event" and since at the period start, paging to the end. If an earlier brief of this kind is visible and the period starts where it ended, use recordedSince there, not since: an event LMTY found late has an older date of its own. If the server ignores recordedSince, read the last 30 days with since and drop the eventIds that brief listed. Say how many of each you read, back to which date, and which competitors were not refreshed in the period. If the latest refresh is more than a week before the period ends, give its date in the first line and say nothing after it is covered.
3. Pick the three items that touch the priorities, or without them that rank highest on business impact, evidence strength, time sensitivity and how costly a wrong call would be. Say the selection is yours and what decided it.
4. For each, call get_evidence or get_market_event, and read the competitor's public profile (search_profiles, then get_profile with sections ["timeline", "pricing"]) for a date of the move's own and its values.
5. Write: a Read line with the counts; the answer in 3 to 5 sentences; three items, each with what happened (who says it, the date and how it is known), why it matters marked as your reading, the source, and a decision question naming the evidence that would answer it.
6. Then at most three risks, each tied to an item; at most three openings, worded as hypotheses; what is not yet worth reacting to, which is the only place for an item resting on one unverified post, with what would settle it; an appendix of claim, source, date and confidence.
7. If nothing in the period touches the priorities, say so in one sentence and give only what is not worth reacting to and the questions that stand regardless.

Rules: A change record's asOf is when LMTY recorded it: "recorded on". It does not place a move in this quarter. Word an event's date by atBasis: occurred is when it happened, published "reported on", observed "seen on". LMTY's significance and implication are its judgments, cited as LMTY's. No motives. No "we should" or "do not": write the decision and the evidence it needs. A competitor's own figure is its claim. "No change recorded" is not "stable". Nothing from memory. A fact you read outside LMTY is marked "my own read of [page], [date]" and never replaces the record. One page; two for a board.

playbooks.title: Launch Readiness
playbooks.when: On demand. Weekly in the last weeks before a launch date. A repeat run should lead with what moved in the decision set since the last run and which posture or claim it changes.
playbooks.summary: Check a launch against the competitors that matter, see where it is ahead, level or behind, and which claims will hold up.
playbooks.delivers: The competitors that matter and why, where the release stands on each point buyers weigh, claims to make and to qualify with their evidence, and up to five gaps to close before launch.

inputs.name: RELEASE
inputs.description: What is shipping and who it is for, in a short paragraph
inputs.example: Audit log export for admins on the Business plan, so security teams can hand evidence to their auditors

inputs.name: LAUNCH_DATE
inputs.description: The day it goes out, if one is set

inputs.name: COMPETITORS
inputs.description: The competitors you want it compared with. Leave empty to pick from the ones you track

examples: Pressure-test this launch against our competitors.
Here is the PRD. What do I need to know competitively before we launch?
Build the competitive section of my launch brief.
Northwind just shipped something similar. Does that change how we should launch this?
Tell me whether this is parity, catch-up, or real differentiation.
We launch in three weeks. Has anything moved with Northwind or Initech since last week?
playbooks.playbook:
Check this launch against the competitors that matter: {RELEASE}. Launch date: {LAUNCH_DATE}. Compare with: {COMPETITORS}.

Use the LMTY MCP tools (`https://mcp.lmty.com/mcp`), signed in. Call search_profiles for the competitors I named before list_products. If list_products asks for sign-in or returns no product, that is not a lost connection: read them with get_profile, say there is no tracked set or change history, and ask who our product is if the release does not say. If {RELEASE} is only a feature's name, ask what ships and for whom, and stop.

1. Restate the release as one claim: what changed, for whom, what job it improves.
2. Call list_products, then list_competitors. Use the ones I named, or pick at most 5 that matter for this release. Say why each, how many of the tracked set that is, and who was left out.
3. Call get_report one `section` at a time for the capability, positioning and pricing. Keys: products_capabilities, positioning_differentiators, pricing_packaging. Call get_freshness for each competitor's as-of date.
4. Call get_report_changes with since 90 days back and limit 50, then the next page while nextCursor is not null. Say whether the history reaches that far, and how many were read. A change's date is when LMTY recorded it: write "recorded on".
5. For each picked competitor: get_market_feed with its competitorId, family "event" and `since` 90 days back (on a repeat run, `recordedSince` the last run's date). Then search_profiles (confirm by website), get_profile sections ["timeline", "facts"] for dated launches and its own taglines and proof points, and get_calendar with upcomingOnly for what is announced near the launch date. Word each date by its `atBasis`: occurred is the event's date, published is "reported on", observed is "seen on".
6. For each competitor capability say shipped, announced or only marketed, and who says so: "Northwind's page states", not "Northwind has".
7. Class each dimension as Category expectation, Parity, Differentiated, Catch-up, Unproven or Vulnerable, saying what the label means. Where the competitor side is only silence, write "not observed in the sources read, as of" the date, and class it Unproven.
8. At most 5 claims we can support, each with its evidence and date; at most 5 to avoid or qualify, each with what would make it supportable; at most 5 gaps before launch.
9. Say what was not read. With no source on a competitor I named, say so, and offer once, at the end, to work in what I can paste about it: its pages, release notes, deal notes.

If you have run this before for this release, lead with what moved since then and which posture or claim it changes. An earlier run is one in this conversation or your client's memory: do not search files. With none, this run is the baseline.

Write: Freshness line | The release in customer terms | Decision set (table) | Where the launch stands (table) | Claims to support | Claims to avoid or qualify | Gaps before launch | Not read.

Rules: Nothing about a competitor from memory: every price, plan, date and wording comes from a tool result, from what I gave you, or from a page you read now, marked as your own reading with its link and the date read. What was not found is "not observed", never "has no", "the only" or "first". Never say who shipped first on a recorded or first-seen date. LMTY's `implication` and `significanceScore` are its judgments: cite them as LMTY's. No motive for any competitor. A post or review is one person's account, never "customers expect". Postures and claims are your judgment: give the evidence each rests on.

playbooks.title: Market Briefing
playbooks.when: Weekly, or monthly for a quieter market. A repeat run should lead with what LMTY recorded since the last briefing and what moved among the items it reported.
playbooks.summary: Brief your team on what changed across your tracked competitors this week, ranked, with a date and a source for each item.
playbooks.delivers: Up to three items, each with what changed, its date and source, and why it may matter; a short watchlist; the competitors with nothing new; and how much was read.

inputs.name: PRODUCT
inputs.description: Your product, if your LMTY account has more than one

inputs.name: PERIOD
inputs.description: The period to cover, if not the last 7 days

examples: Give me this week's competitive briefing.
What changed across our competitors in August?
What should sales learn this week about the competitive landscape?
Turn LMTY's latest changes into a Slack-ready PMM update.
What mattered this month and what should we keep watching?
Every Monday, post a competitive briefing to our team channel.
playbooks.playbook:
Brief me on what changed across my product's tracked competitors. Product: {PRODUCT}. Period: {PERIOD}. If either is blank: the one product on my account, the last 7 days.

Use the LMTY MCP tools (`https://mcp.lmty.com/mcp`), signed in to my account. A sign-in request is not a lost connection: say once that this needs my account, and stop. Call list_products first. With several products and none named, list them in one line and stop. With none, ask which product and competitors to cover, and stop.

1. Look for the last briefing in this conversation or your client's memory; never search files. With one, start the period where its "Covered" line ends. With none on a scheduled run, open with "The previous briefing could not be seen: this covers [dates]" and use no continuity labels.
2. Call list_competitors, get_freshness and get_recent_activity. Note competitors not refreshed in the period, paused refreshes, and competitors added in it: their records are first captures, not changes. LMTY's record begins at the oldest get_recent_activity entry, paged to the end: if that is inside the period, say so in the first line, and what LMTY captured that day is what it held, not a change.
3. Call get_market_feed with family "event" and recordedSince at the period start, paging until nextCursor is null. Say "N events read". If the server ignores recordedSince, read the last 30 days with since and drop the eventIds the last briefing listed.
4. Call get_report_changes with since at the period start and limit 50, then the next page while nextCursor is not null. Skip `created` entries. Say how many you read and back to which date. If you stop sooner, the period is what you reached.
5. Merge entries about one change. Leave out what the last briefing reported unless it moved. Before calling an item new, check that competitor's earlier change records and profile timeline; if they hold it, say when LMTY first recorded it. Rank by relevance to my product, magnitude, novelty, time sensitivity and evidence quality, and say the order is yours.
6. At most 3 items (5 for a month). Each: what the source says, its date and how it is known, the source link (get_market_event or get_evidence), and why it may matter, marked as your reading. For a date of its own and before and after values, read the competitor's public profile: search_profiles, confirm by its website, then get_profile with sections ["pricing", "timeline"].
7. At most 3 watchlist items. Then each competitor with no change recorded, with its last refresh date.
8. End with "Covered: [start] to [end, UTC]. Event ids reported: [ids]." Nothing follows it.

If nothing new was recorded: the period, the coverage line, "No change recorded since [date]", the competitors not refreshed, the Covered line, and stop. If nothing was refreshed in the period, give the last refresh of the report and of each competitor after the period line, say the period is not covered, and end the Covered line at the latest refresh.

Rules: A change record's asOf is when LMTY recorded it: write "recorded on". Word an event's date by atBasis: occurred is when it happened, published is "reported on", observed is "seen on" and never "new" or "this week". LMTY's significance and implication are its judgments: quote them as LMTY's and never rank on them. No motives. "No change recorded" is never "quiet" or "stable". A competitor's claim about itself is its statement. Nothing from memory. A fact you read outside LMTY is marked "my own read of [page], [date]" with its link, and never replaces the record. Under 400 words outside the table.

playbooks.title: Market Shift Analysis
playbooks.when: On demand, when a pattern of signals needs a verdict, and monthly for a hypothesis being watched. A repeat run should lead with whether the classification moved and which signal moved it.
playbooks.summary: Test whether a trend you are seeing across competitors is real, how far the evidence goes, and what would change the answer.
playbooks.delivers: A verdict from noise to established expectation, with the bar it did not clear, a dated list of signals, what would prove it wrong, and three signals to watch next.

inputs.name: HYPOTHESIS
inputs.description: The trend you want tested, in your own words
inputs.example: Everyone is moving AI features into their base plans

inputs.name: COMPANIES
inputs.description: Companies to include beyond your tracked competitors, or the ones to read if you are not signed in

inputs.name: BUYER_EVIDENCE
inputs.description: What your buyers have said or done about it, pasted in - call notes, lost-deal reasons, survey answers
inputs.example: 4 of the last 20 enterprise RFPs asked for AI in the base plan

examples: Everyone is adding AI. Is this actually a market shift or just noise?
Three competitors changed packaging. What is happening?
Are we seeing a real move upmarket in this category?
What would have to happen before we treat this as table stakes?
Analyze the last 90 days of changes and tell me which patterns are real.
Northwind and Initech both started calling themselves an operations platform. Is the category moving?
playbooks.playbook:
Tell me whether this is a real market shift: {HYPOTHESIS}. Also read: {COMPANIES}. Buyer evidence: {BUYER_EVIDENCE}.

What this prompt cannot do: it cannot see our deals or calls. LMTY holds no buyer evidence, so without buyer evidence pasted above the verdict cannot pass "Emerging shift". Say so in the first lines when that is the case.

Use the LMTY MCP tools (`https://mcp.lmty.com/mcp`).

1. Restate the hypothesis as one falsifiable sentence and say the framing is yours. Go on without waiting.
2. For each company in the pattern, call search_profiles, confirm it by its website, and call get_profile with sections ["terms", "timeline", "pricing"] (add "hiring" or "statements" when the hypothesis is about those). Then call list_products and list_competitors; if they ask for sign-in or return nothing, that is not a lost connection: work from the companies named above.
3. Signed in: call get_report_changes with since at the period start and limit 50, then the next page while nextCursor is not null, and get_market_feed with family "event", paging to the end. Say how many records you read, back to which date, and K of M companies read. A company not read is "not read". If the oldest get_recent_activity entry, paged to the end, falls inside the period, say first that LMTY's record begins on that date.
4. Build a ledger of at most 12 signals: date and how it is known, signal, source, independent or not, evidence quality. Merge signals that trace to one event. Include signals from outside the tracked set, and say the analysis was not restricted to it.
5. Classify, starting at Noise. Isolated move: one credible dated signal. Emerging shift: independent subjects, and at least one signal from a source other than the vendors themselves (press, an analyst, a customer); a vendor's own page, docs or post is a vendor source, so several vendors each describing their own move stay Isolated move. Accelerating: that plus buyer-side evidence. Established: buyers screen for it. Cap at the weakest link.
6. Say which bar was not met and what would clear it, what would falsify the reading, and three signals to watch with where to look and when.

Rules: A change record's asOf is when LMTY recorded it, and an observed date is when LMTY first saw a thing: both count toward how many players have it, never toward timing or "accelerating". A reported-on date places the report, not the move, and shows no sequence. Say how many signals have a date of their own. A vendor's page is primary for what it offers and charges; what it says about its customers is its own claim, never buyer evidence. Posts are people saying something: count posts and authors, never customers. Noise means the evidence read shows no pattern, not that there is none. No motives. Name decisions; do not make them. Nothing from memory. A signal you read outside LMTY is marked "my own read of [page], [date]" in its source and never alone lifts the verdict.

playbooks.title: Messaging Audit
playbooks.when: Quarterly, and on demand when copy is about to ship or a competitor relaunches. A repeat run should lead with claims whose mark changed since the last audit and competitor wording first recorded since then.
playbooks.summary: Test whether your homepage or message still sets you apart from what competitors now say, and see which questions are really about positioning.
playbooks.delivers: Your message laid out by layer, each claim marked still distinct, converged or parity, with competitors' wording quoted and dated, what was not tested, and up to seven changes to consider.

inputs.name: MESSAGE
inputs.description: Paste the homepage, message hierarchy, pitch or campaign copy to test
inputs.example: Our homepage hero and the three sections under it, pasted below

inputs.name: COMPETITORS
inputs.description: The competitors to compare against. Leave it empty to use the ones you track in LMTY

examples: Review our homepage messaging. Does it still differentiate us?
Does our messaging still reflect the market?
Northwind and Initech started saying 'AI-native' too. What did that break in our message?
Pressure-test this message hierarchy against how customers actually talk.
Check this campaign copy against our positioning before it ships.
How do people word our category in public posts, compared with our homepage?
playbooks.playbook:
Audit this message against what competitors now say. Do not rewrite it.

Message: {MESSAGE}
Competitors to compare against: {COMPETITORS}

Use the LMTY MCP tools (`https://mcp.lmty.com/mcp`), signed in to my LMTY account. A sign-in request is not a lost connection: say once that this needs my account, and stop.

1. Call list_products and list_competitors. Lay the message out by layer: category, value, differentiation, proof, call to action, and the audience it seems to address. Note structural findings, such as differentiation with no proof.
2. For each competitor (the ones I named, else the tracked set): get_freshness for its own as-of date, and get_report one section at a time, starting with positioning and differentiators (take the key from the answer).
3. For each one's own wording: search_profiles, confirm by website, then get_profile for the overview, then the facts section with factKinds ["tagline", "category_claim", "proof_point", "boilerplate"], and the terms section. A competitor I do not track is read from its profile alone.
4. For each differentiation and value claim: who else says it, quoted with page and date, out of how many competitors read. Mark it still distinct (not found in the [n] of [m] read, as of their dates) | converged | parity stated as difference.
5. Give "since" only from a date of the wording's own: the earliest known use of a term, the end date of wording it replaced, a dated launch. Otherwise write "on record since [date]; when they began is not known". get_report_changes and get_market_feed with family "event" show what moved, dated by when LMTY recorded or read it: never say who said it first from that order.
6. Where wording converged, do the products still differ? A capability known only from a competitor's own pages is "unknown: their own claim only".
7. Customer fit: test the message's words against calls or interviews I pasted. With none, and if you can open review-site pages now, test against public reviews of my product and these competitors: each quote labeled "third-party opinion: review on [site], [date], one reviewer's account", never "customers say" or a count of customers, and say the customer side rests on public reviews alone. With neither, say it was not tested and what would test it.
8. Up to seven changes to consider, labeled as your judgment, each with its evidence and a confidence with its reason. List separately the findings that are really about the position, for competitive-positioning.

Open with: competitor wording read for [n] of [m] tracked competitors; customer evidence: [what I gave you, or none]; public reviews: [n read and on which sites, or none].

If you have audited this message before, lead with claims whose mark changed since then and wording first recorded since then, reading events with recordedSince from that date. With no earlier run in view, say this one is the baseline.

Rules: Convergence is about words, not products. Quote competitor wording as written, with page and date, and say whether it came from the report or the profile. Nothing from memory: wording or dates only from a tool result, my material or a page read now; a page read outside LMTY is marked as your own reading with its link and date read, and never replaces wording LMTY holds. "Still distinct" is about the competitors read, never the market. A contradicted claim names the source that contradicts it; whether to remove it is my call. Do not re-decide the position, and do not read public posts unless I ask.

playbooks.title: Objection Response
playbooks.when: On demand.
playbooks.summary: Answer a buyer's objection about a competitor - check whether it's true, then get one thing to say, one question to ask, and what not to claim.
playbooks.delivers: The objection checked against current facts with source and date, a 15-second response, one or two questions to ask, proof if you have it, what not to say, and where the competitor may be stronger.

inputs.name: OBJECTION
inputs.description: What the buyer said, in their words if you have them
inputs.example: Northwind has way more integrations than you

inputs.name: COMPETITOR
inputs.description: The competitor the objection is about, if the objection doesn't name it

inputs.name: PROOF
inputs.description: Paste any approved proof you can use, such as documentation or a customer story you're cleared to share
inputs.example: Our integrations page, updated 1 November, lists native connectors for the buyer's ticketing and identity systems

examples: The buyer just said Northwind has more integrations. What do I say?
Globex says Initech is 30% cheaper. How should the rep respond?
Our prospect told us we don't have audit logging. We do. How do I handle it?
The Globex security team says Northwind is more secure. Help.
Buyer says Northwind deploys in a week. Is that true, and what do I ask?
A rep wants to tell the team we always win on implementation against Initech. Can they, and what should they say to this buyer?
playbooks.playbook:
A buyer said: "{OBJECTION}". The competitor, if the objection doesn't name it: {COMPETITOR}. Approved proof I can use: {PROOF}

Use the LMTY MCP tools (`https://mcp.lmty.com/mcp`), signed in to my account. Call search_profiles for a company named here before list_products. If list_products asks for sign-in or returns no product, that is not a lost connection: say so once, ask which product is mine, and use public profiles only.

1. Write the objection as given. If I paraphrased, mark it as a paraphrase.
2. Call list_products, then list_competitors to resolve the competitor. If none can be identified, ask one question listing the tracked names and stop.
3. Check the premise, about six reads: get_evidence with its competitorId for the signal that bears on it (with confidence and dates), and one get_report section. search_profiles for the competitor, confirmed by website, then get_profile: the overview for plans on sale, ["pricing"] for dated price moves, ["facts"] with factKinds certification, proof_point or reported_price, ["connections"] with connectionKinds ["integrates_with"] for integrations. Only if the objection is about a change: get_market_feed with family "event" and its competitorId.
4. Give one label: verified, partly verified, not supported by the sources checked, or unknown, with source, date and LMTY's confidence (none is unknown, not false). A claim only the competitor makes about itself is its own claim. If unknown, name what would check it.
5. The concern underneath, only as far as the buyer's words support.
6. A 15-second response a person could say.
7. One or two questions that change what happens next.
8. Proof only from what I pasted; otherwise "no approved proof supplied".
9. What not to say, and where they may be stronger.

Rules: A count on LMTY's record is how many LMTY has read, never the product's total: write "N known to LMTY, read N of M", and do not rule on "more" from two counts. The list price is the plan on sale now; what someone says they pay is one person's account. Not found is "not observed in the sources checked, as of [date]", never "they don't have". An event's date by its atBasis: "reported on" for published, "seen on" for observed, never "just". A `date` in the price history (`pricingHistory`) has no basis until its event is read by `eventId` (get_market_event): until then "dated [date] in LMTY's price history". Nothing from memory, reputation included. A page read outside LMTY is marked in place with its link and date read, and never the only basis for the line I say. LMTY's view of my product is not proof. One deal is one deal. Read no public posts. If I also asked for a comparison document, say no skill here writes one; anything for the buyer is a draft.

playbooks.title: POC and RFP Plan
playbooks.when: On demand, once per evaluation; weekly while one is running. A repeat run should lead with the proof events settled since the last run, the unknowns resolved, and any no-go condition now met.
playbooks.summary: Plan a POC or bake-off against a competitor - which requirements decide it, what to prove, where they're stronger, and when not to compete.
playbooks.delivers: The buyer's requirements sorted into mandatory, table stakes, deciding and irrelevant, both sides of each deciding one with who says so, a proof plan, questions to ask, and when to walk away.

inputs.name: COMPETITOR
inputs.description: The competitor in the evaluation, as you track it in LMTY

inputs.name: REQUIREMENTS
inputs.description: Paste the buyer's requirements or scoring criteria, up to a page. Leave it empty if the buyer hasn't stated any yet
inputs.example: 1. SSO with our identity provider (mandatory). 2. Audit log export to our security tools (weight 20%). 3. Go-live in 30 days.

inputs.name: EVALUATION
inputs.description: What kind of evaluation it is, the timeline, and who decides
inputs.example: four-week POC, starting 1 December, IT director decides

examples: We're going into a POC against Northwind at Globex next month. What should we prove?
Globex sent their RFP. Help us shape the response against Initech.
Draft our answers to this security questionnaire from our approved docs.
Here's the buyer's scoring matrix. Which criteria will decide it?
Globex just said 'let's do a POV'. Nothing else yet. How do we set it up?
Should we even bid on this RFP? The requirements read like Northwind wrote them.
playbooks.playbook:
Plan our evaluation against {COMPETITOR}. Evaluation: {EVALUATION}. The buyer's requirements:

{REQUIREMENTS}

Use the LMTY MCP tools (`https://mcp.lmty.com/mcp`), signed in to my account. Call search_profiles for a company named here before list_products. If list_products asks for sign-in or returns no product, that is not a lost connection: say so once, ask which product is mine, and use public profiles only. This prompt carries only what I pasted: a long written RFP does not fit here, and our side comes only from approved documentation I paste.

1. Call list_products, then list_competitors to match {COMPETITOR}. If it is not tracked, read it from its public profile alone and say so.
2. State the objective in two lines: what the evaluation decides, who decides, by when.
3. If no requirements are pasted, give the short form: the objective, questions that would establish criteria with the buyer, and no-go conditions only where my words give evidence, else "none established yet", then the unknowns to resolve. Say in the first line that no requirements were given. Stop there.
4. List the requirements with source and one class each: mandatory (pass/fail, the buyer's word), table stakes, differentiating, or irrelevant to this buyer, with the basis for each class. One the sponsor says was inherited or suggested by the incumbent is "candidate irrelevant", with a question for the next call. A mandatory one whose fit only the buyer can rule on stays mandatory, marked "for the buyer to rule on", with a question for the next call; never a "yes". Say how many there are and how many were read.
5. Per differentiating criterion, the competitor side: get_evidence with its competitorId, the matching get_report section, get_freshness; search_profiles, confirmed by website, then get_profile ["facts"] with factKinds certification, or ["connections"] with connectionKinds ["integrates_with"], read N of M. Each line says who states it: "the vendor states (its page, last seen [date])", or "reported by". A certification is always "the vendor states".
6. Our side only from what I pasted; otherwise "needs approved documentation".
7. A proof event per differentiator: what the buyer sees, who runs it, what pass looks like.
8. Up to five questions that expose trade-offs, none that works only if the buyer is misled. A question for the buyer is something said to the buyer: it carries no claim my pasted documentation does not support.
9. Where they are stronger, and whether the buyer called it decisive; what we win that the buyer has not weighted, not to overplay.
10. No-go conditions the evidence supports, each with its source.

Rules: The buyer's requirements are the criteria, not the competitor's feature list. Nothing about either product from memory, and nothing from what buyers usually ask for. Not found is "not observed in the sources checked, as of [date]", never "they don't have". A page read outside LMTY is marked in place with its link and date read. Mark classifications and no-go conditions as your judgment. If I ask for RFP answers, draft only what my pasted documentation supports, as drafts for the bid owner, marking every workaround, security answer and timeline commitment for confirmation; never a "yes" to a partial fit.

playbooks.title: Pricing and Packaging Review
playbooks.when: On demand, when a pricing or packaging decision is open. Worth repeating each quarter before a pricing review. A repeat run should lead with the cells of the offer map that changed since the last run and the moves recorded since then.
playbooks.summary: Compare your pricing and packaging with the competitors that matter, and get the questions to settle before you change a price.
playbooks.delivers: What each competitor lists today and how its prices have moved, with dates, where your offer is ahead or exposed, up to five hypotheses to test, and up to five questions for the pricing team.

inputs.name: DECISION
inputs.description: The pricing or packaging question you are deciding
inputs.example: Whether to respond to Northwind's lower entry price

inputs.name: HOME_PRICING
inputs.description: Your current plans and prices, or the change you are proposing. Paste them in
inputs.example: Starter $20 per seat a month, Business $45, Enterprise on request

inputs.name: COMPETITORS
inputs.description: The competitors to compare with. Leave empty to pick from the ones you track

examples: Northwind raised prices. What should we examine before changing ours?
Compare our packaging against these six competitors and pressure-test our new plan structure.
Are we charging separately for something the market treats as table stakes?
Build a pricing and packaging review for the exec team.
What changed in competitor pricing over the last quarter and what questions should it raise for us?
Should we match Initech's lower entry price?
playbooks.playbook:
Review our pricing and packaging for this decision: {DECISION}. Our pricing: {HOME_PRICING}. Compare with: {COMPETITORS}.

Use the LMTY MCP tools (`https://mcp.lmty.com/mcp`), signed in. Call search_profiles for a company named here before list_products. If list_products asks for sign-in or returns no product, that is not a lost connection: read the competitors I named from their public profiles, say there is no tracked set or change history, and take our offer from what I pasted.

1. Say what kind of decision this is: a scan, a reaction to a competitor move, a new price point, a packaging redesign, a free-to-paid boundary, an entitlement, a segment offer or launch pricing.
2. Call list_products and list_competitors. Use the ones I named, or pick at most 6 that matter; say how many of the tracked set that is and who was left out.
3. For each, call search_profiles for the product (prices sit on the product, not the company; confirm by website), then get_profile for the overview: the `pricing_plan` facts are the plans on sale, with the date last seen. Write prices as listed; do not convert units.
4. Call get_profile with sections ["pricing"] and page with offset until `more` is empty: the history is under `pricingHistory`, as `changes` and `ended`. A change's `date` has no basis: read its event by `eventId` (get_market_event) to learn whose date it is (the move's own, "reported on", or "seen on"); otherwise write "dated [date] in LMTY's price history". Say where each record begins. A plan first seen on a date was not introduced on it. Write "no change observed between" two dates, never "has not changed".
5. Call get_report with `section` "pricing_packaging", and get_report_changes with since at the start of the period I care about and limit 50, then the next page while nextCursor is not null, saying how far back you read. A change's date is when LMTY recorded it: write "recorded on".
6. Build the offer map. A capability the pricing page does not mention is "not listed on the pricing page as of" the date; a plan with no public price is "contact sales: no public price"; no pricing on record is "not observed", never "none", "free" or "custom". What people report paying (`reported_price`) goes in a note, never in a price cell.
7. Mark where our offer is a price advantage, value advantage, clearer packaging, exposed (and against whom), intentionally premium, or a false comparison, with the evidence for each.
8. At most 5 hypotheses, each with the internal evidence that would confirm or reject it, and at most 5 decision questions.
9. Say what was not read.

Write: Freshness line | Offer map (table) | Moves (table) | Our offer | Hypotheses | Decision questions | Limitations.

Rules: No price, plan or limit from memory, however well known the vendor: each comes from a tool result, from what I pasted, or from a page you read now, marked as your own reading with its link and the date read, and never in place of a price LMTY holds. A list price is what a page said on a date, not what anyone paid. No motive for a competitor's price move. Without our margins and deal data, do not answer yes or no: "do not match" and "hold" are recommendations too. Open with what the evidence shows and the question it leaves, and what would settle it. Hypotheses and diagnoses are your judgment: give the evidence each rests on.

playbooks.title: Roadmap Review
playbooks.when: Quarterly, before planning, for a product area being watched; on demand when a roadmap question is open. A repeat run should lead with competitor movement in the area since the last run and any question whose class changed.
playbooks.summary: Turn what competitors did in one product area, and what your customers say, into questions product can investigate, with what is still unknown.
playbooks.delivers: What competitors did in the area, with dates, your customer evidence beside it, and up to seven questions, each marked as expected, a chance to stand out, noise, or not yet known.

inputs.name: PRODUCT_AREA
inputs.description: The part of your product to review

inputs.name: CUSTOMER_EVIDENCE
inputs.description: What your customers have said or done about this area. Paste feature requests, interview notes or usage figures, with how many you looked through
inputs.example: Reporting came up in 6 of 40 support tickets in October; 3 of 12 lost deals named it

examples: What should product investigate in reporting, based on the market?
Northwind and Initech keep adding AI assistants. Does that matter for our roadmap?
Review our Q3 roadmap against market and customer evidence.
Are we missing something important in admin and permissions?
Competitors all launched audit logs this year. Is that table stakes for us?
playbooks.playbook:
Review {PRODUCT_AREA} against what competitors did and what our customers say. Our customer evidence: {CUSTOMER_EVIDENCE}.

Use the LMTY MCP tools (`https://mcp.lmty.com/mcp`), signed in. Call search_profiles for any competitor I name first. If list_products asks for sign-in or returns no product, that is not a lost connection: read their public profiles, say there is no tracked set, and ask which product is ours. LMTY holds the market side only: our customers' side is what I pasted. Without it, every question is an evidence gap.

1. Restate the area as the customer need it serves, not as a competitor feature.
2. Call list_products and list_competitors. Say how many of the tracked set you read.
3. Call get_report with the `section` that covers the area (products_capabilities, positioning_differentiators, pricing_packaging, gtm_motion, partnerships_ecosystem, customers_solutions or compliance_trust), then get_report_changes with since about a quarter back and limit 50, then the next page while nextCursor is not null; say whether the history reaches that far and how many were read. A change's date is when LMTY recorded it: write "recorded on".
4. For each tracked competitor: get_market_feed with its competitorId, family "event" and since a quarter back (on a repeat run, `recordedSince` the last run's date), judging each event by its content: search matches words literally and misses a release named otherwise, so use it only to narrow. For each that moved, call search_profiles (confirm by website) and get_profile sections ["timeline", "pricing", "hiring"]. Say shipped, announced or only marketed, the plan it landed in, and each date by its `atBasis`: occurred is the event's date, published is "reported on", observed is "seen on".
5. Say whether order of movement can be established. On recorded or first-seen dates write "order not established" and do not say who followed whom.
6. Set my customer evidence beside it, counted, with how many were searched and what that sample cannot speak to.
7. At most 7 questions, each a customer problem, never "build X". Mark each: table-stakes risk (needs evidence that its absence costs deals or renewals), differentiator opportunity, copycat noise (competitors moving, no buyer evidence), or evidence gap. If our product meets the need differently and my evidence supports that, say so; it is not a gap.
8. For each, the evidence missing before anyone could prioritize it. Do not rank the questions.
9. Say what was not read.

If you have run this before for {PRODUCT_AREA}, lead with competitor movement since then and any question whose mark changed. An earlier run is one in this conversation or your client's memory: do not search files. With none, this run is the baseline.

Write: Read line | Market signals (table) | Our customer evidence | Questions (table: question, mark, evidence, evidence missing) | Not read.

Rules: Nothing about a competitor from memory: each move comes from a tool result, from what I pasted, or from a page you read now, marked as your own reading with its link and the date read. How hard a vendor sells something (its pricing page, a tier gate, its own customer stories) is its own claim, not buyer evidence. A review or post is one person's account: count reviews, never buyers, and label a review "third-party opinion: review on [site], [date], one reviewer's account". Never infer our customers' demand from competitors. "Competitors have not solved it" needs a source; otherwise "not observed in the sources read". No motive for any competitor. Every mark is your judgment: give its evidence.

playbooks.title: Competitor Change Impact
playbooks.when: On demand, when a change lands. Daily for the two weeks after a change that matters. A repeat run should lead with posts since the last run, and say when it found no new posts.
playbooks.summary: See how a competitor's change is landing in public: who's reporting problems, who says they're switching, and who's unaffected.
playbooks.delivers: The change and its date, post counts before and after where collection allows, quoted posts sorted into experience, intent, questions, and opinion, and what it could cause beside what posts report.

inputs.name: COMPETITOR
inputs.description: A competitor you track in LMTY

inputs.name: CHANGE
inputs.description: The change to trace
inputs.example: closing the cheapest plan to new customers

examples: Northwind closed its cheapest plan last week. How are their customers reacting?
Is anyone looking to switch away from Northwind after the price increase?
Initech just got acquired. What are its users saying?
Who is complaining about Northwind's new usage limits?
Northwind's redesign shipped Monday. Is this an opening for us?
playbooks.playbook:
Show me how this change at {COMPETITOR} is landing in public: {CHANGE}.

Use the LMTY MCP tools (`https://mcp.lmty.com/mcp`), signed in with Social Listening on. If a tool asks for sign-in or says it is off, tell me once and stop.

1. Call list_products and list_competitors: if {COMPETITOR} is not tracked, say its posts were not collected; stop.
2. Date the change: get_market_feed with the competitorId and family "event", then get_market_event for its sources. A published date can be a commentator's: if search_profiles finds {COMPETITOR}, check get_profile sections ["pricing", "changes"] for an earlier one. Use the earliest date a source supports (the first stage if staged); give its source and `atBasis`, and say so if my date differs. Only observed, or only commentators as sources: no before and after, just posts since then. Not in the feed: use my description, date unconfirmed.
3. Count After: get_mention_stats with the competitorId, from 00:00 UTC on the change's day to now, max 30 days. If the answer's `competitorId` is null it counted my whole product: say so, no period counts. Collection began on the latest `since` in `platformsSince` among platforms with a tenth or more of `byPlatform`. No period begins before that or over 90 days back: move After's start there and say so. Before is as long and ends where After begins: if too early, shorten both; if none is left, leave it empty and call nothing a rise or a fall.
4. Show both periods: `totalRelevantMentions`, `distinctAuthors`, `bySentiment`, `byTag`, and a per-day average over whole UTC days of `byDay`, never `windowDays`; a part day is a count with its hours. If a platform with a tenth or more of After has none before, name it, give counts only, call nothing a rise. No percentage if either is under 20; no cause. These are keyword matches, not posts about {COMPETITOR}, and a floor.
5. Read list_mentions with the competitorId over After before shortening: at most 5 pages per filter, never splitting the period. Untagged first: 2 pages if over 5 pages. If `nextCursor` is not null, add the `byTag` tags with most posts that bear on the change. One untagged Before page for topics if Before is comparable. For each, say the hours or days covered and "read N of M": N mentions received, M that filter's count. Keep only posts whose `matchedKeywords` name {COMPETITOR}.
6. Keep posts whose excerpt names the change. Keep as "inferred from timing and content", counted apart, only those describing its direct effect without naming it. Same topic, another reason or none: "same topic, change not named", not reaction; give both counts. Drop tags first_party, directory, promotional_post and ai_generated.
7. Group each kept post once: Reported experience (first-hand, good or bad) | Stated intent (leaving, evaluating, seeking an alternative) | Question | Opinion or prediction | Unaffected or in favor. Quote up to 5 a group, max 200 characters, with platform, date, link and `author`. Write intent as "says they cancelled", never as the act.
8. Table: what a change like this could cause | what posts report, with counts or empty. Say if one thread holds over half.

Rules: a post is one person's account, an author a handle: count posts and authors, never customers. No motive for the competitor, no churn forecast. Nothing found is "not observed in what LMTY collects", never "no reaction". Web search only for the change on {COMPETITOR}'s own pages; never count web posts. Contact nobody: a reply I ask for is a draft. With few or no posts, give only the counts, days read and what was not observed.

playbooks.title: Keyword Check
playbooks.when: Monthly, and whenever you add a competitor. A repeat run should start with what changed in your keyword list since the last run.
playbooks.summary: Check whether the keywords LMTY tracks for you still catch the right posts, and which ones catch too little or the wrong posts.
playbooks.delivers: It lists names and handles your keywords don't cover yet, keywords that match few posts or the wrong ones, and keywords to clean up, like paused ones or ones for competitors you no longer track. It also flags tracked competitors with no keywords, shows what changed in your list, and suggests up to 7 changes to make in LMTY.
examples: Are we still tracking the right keywords?
Review our social listening setup. What are we missing?
Northwind renamed its product in the spring. Are we still catching mentions of it?
Why do we get so few mentions of Initech?
Our keyword 'pilot' seems to pull in a lot of junk. Is it worth keeping?
We just added a competitor. Do its keywords cover everything it sells?
playbooks.playbook:
Check whether the phrases LMTY monitors for my product still cover the right things.

Use the LMTY MCP tools (`https://mcp.lmty.com/mcp`), signed in with Social Listening on. If a tool asks for sign-in or says it is off, tell me once and offer this instead: I paste my phrases and competitors, and you find the gaps against public profiles. At most 35 calls. Read-only: you list changes and make none.

1. Call list_products (ask which if several), then list_competitors.
2. Call list_tracked_keywords. Count the phrases by `kind`, those with `status` paused, and the `removed` list.
3. Call get_mention_stats twice, for 90 and 30 days: keep `byKeyword` and `listeningSince`. If listening began under 90 days ago, say how many days the 90-day count covers.
4. For my product, then competitors in list_competitors order (those an earlier run did not reach first), while calls last: search_profiles; get_profile on the profile with exactly that name, sections ["overview", "facts"], factKinds ["former_name"], for its `website`, its `channels` with `role` product or company, and former names; then sections ["connections"], connectionKinds ["offers", "acquired"]. A company's `offers` ties are its products. A product's `offers` tie pointing in names its maker: if graded above chatter, read the maker's connections the same way. Otherwise say "no maker on record" or give the chatter tie as such, and never take a maker or product name from `related`, the search or a shared name. Say which subjects you read of how many: the rest, any with no profile, and my product if no profile has exactly its name, are "not checked".
5. Gaps, at most 12: a thing on the record that no active or paused phrase equals or is contained in. Give its grade and date ("seen since" unless a start is stated; never "new"; "not given" for a website or channel) and the phrase to add, spelled as the record spells it. Never propose a name from memory.
6. Quiet phrases, at most 10: `byKeyword` for 30 and 90 days beside the days since `addedAt`, or since listening began if later. Under 14 days: "too new to judge". None: "no posts matched in N days of monitoring", never "dead".
7. For up to 3 phrases that look like common words: one list_mentions page each with includeLowRelevance true, and the competitorId if it is a competitor's. Keep posts whose `matchedKeywords` include the phrase and say how many are about its subject, as numbers, from their openings. A phrase you did not read is never called noisy.
8. Loose ends: `kind` competitor with `competitorId` null (the rival is not tracked now); a tracked competitor with no phrase; paused phrases. Give a pause no date.
9. What changed: phrases by `addedAt` and `removed` by `removedAt`, since my last run, or in the last 30 and 90 days, one row per batch of one day. A count that differs across such a date is a change in collection, not in conversation.
10. What to change in LMTY: at most 7 options, most useful first, each with the row it comes from and the wrong matches to expect, judged from the phrase: a domain has matched longer domains ending in it, and a short phrase has matched inside other text.

If you have run this before, lead with what changed in the list since then. An earlier run is one you can see in this conversation or in memory your client provides: do not search files or folders for one. With none, this run is the baseline.

Rules: A count is relevant posts that matched a phrase, not posts about its subject. A gap is "on LMTY's record, not among the tracked phrases". Give no reason why a phrase was added, removed or paused.

Give me the weekly social listening brief.

playbooks.playbook:
Brief me on what people posted in public about {PRODUCT}, my product, its competitors and our category in the last 7 days.

Use the LMTY MCP tools (`https://mcp.lmty.com/mcp`). Call search_profiles for {PRODUCT} first, then list_products. If it returns {PRODUCT} and Social Listening is on, do A, in at most 18 calls. Otherwise do B, in at most 8, without asking me to sign in.

A. Signed in:

1. Call list_competitors and list_tracked_keywords. If no phrase has `kind` own_brand, say so before any number: LMTY monitors no phrase for {PRODUCT} itself, so the brief covers competitors. Before any count, name each phrase whose `addedAt` or `removedAt` falls in the period.
2. Call get_mention_stats since 00:00 UTC seven days ago, never before `listeningSince`. Then for up to 5 competitors by competitorId, those with most posts in `byKeyword`.
3. Volume, one row each: `totalRelevantMentions`, `distinctAuthors`, the largest of `byPlatform`, the busiest whole day of `byDay`. Never "spike", "drop" or "quiet": for a whole day under a quarter of the median, say a gap in collection cannot be told from a quiet day.
4. Call list_mentions for the largest tags in `byTag` among churn_intent, buy_intent, product_question, bug_report and negative user_feedback: a page each, then second pages. For each say "read N of M" and the days covered. Say which subject each post matched, from `matchedKeywords` and the phrase list. Drop posts about something else, the subjects' own, promotion and AI-written ones.
5. Themes, at most 5: each a count over all matching posts, with two linked excerpts and the author groups (company, vendor, partner, independent, unknown). Say what the posts say only from 20 or more read by 10 or more authors, as numbers with the days or hours they cover; otherwise list them and write "floor not met".
6. Call get_market_feed once, family "event", kinds price_changed, product_launched, product_deprecated, security_incident, funding_announced, acquisition_announced, partnership_announced, legal_action, company_shutdown, company_renamed. Say "N events read of a feed not counted, from [time] back to [time]"; show at most 5. Set a day's count beside one only if its `atBasis` is occurred. Otherwise "reported on" (published) or "first seen on" (observed); if none is occurred, say so.
7. Needs attention, at most 5: what, why, where next. Questions people ask, above the same floor or when I ask for them: "answered on the record" with the fact, grade and date from get_profile for the product asked about, "not on the record", or "not looked up".

B. Not signed in: for {PRODUCT} and up to 2 of {COMPETITORS}, call search_profiles, then get_profile with sections ["chatter"], then ["timeline"] in its own call, {PRODUCT} first. One row each from `chatterCounts`: if null, "LMTY collects no posts for it" (not "0 posts"); if `posts` is 0, "none collected in the last 30 days" Quote at most 10 posts, by author group: the most engaged of 30 days, not a sample. No themes below the floor. Events: at most 3 each, worded as in step 6; "not read" if not asked for. Say once what an account would add.

If you have run this before, lead with what differs. An earlier run is one in this conversation or your client's memory: never search files. With none, this is the baseline. Call volume a rise or a fall only if both periods began after listening did, with the same platforms and phrases, over whole days.

Rules: Counts are posts that matched a phrase and their authors, never customers or users. Nothing from memory or the web. End with what was not read, with both numbers.

playbooks.playbook:
Find public posts that praise {PRODUCT}, my own product, and might be worth quoting.

Use the LMTY MCP tools (`https://mcp.lmty.com/mcp`), at most 12 calls. Call search_profiles for {PRODUCT} first, then list_products. If it returns {PRODUCT} and Social Listening is on, do A. Otherwise (sign-in asked for, no product, or Social Listening off) do B without asking me to sign in, and say once that an account with Social Listening on adds every collected post, with sentiment and tags.

A. Signed in: call list_tracked_keywords. With no phrase of `kind` own_brand, say LMTY monitors no phrase for {PRODUCT} itself, so praise of it is not collected through this account (and when its own were removed, from `removed`), and do B. Else call get_mention_stats for 30 days with ownOnly true: M is `bySentiment.positive`. Get {PRODUCT}'s `channels` as in B. Call list_mentions with ownOnly true, sentiment positive and limit 50, up to 7 pages. Say "read N of M positive posts that matched my own phrases". If I point at posts instead (a link, an author, a day): read those days with list_mentions, ownOnly only if I have own phrases, and judge only them by steps 1 to 3, with no wider count.

B. Not signed in: call search_profiles for "{PRODUCT}" and take the product's profile (ask if several match). Call get_profile for its overview and its company's: keep `channels`. Call get_profile with sections ["chatter"] for the product, paging until `more` is empty, and for the company only if its overview counts posts. Say "read N of M", M from `chatterCounts.posts`: the most engaged posts of 30 days, not a sample; praise is judged by reading. If `chatterCounts` is null, say LMTY collects no public posts for {PRODUCT}, which is not nobody praising it, and stop. If `posts` is 0, say LMTY collected none in the last 30 days, and stop.

Then, either way:

1. Keep a post only if its excerpt itself praises {PRODUCT}: not praise of someone else that only names it, a kind word inside a complaint, or praise that may come after the cut.
2. Sort each author: the company (a handle in `channels` under any role but community, or one who says they work there), a partner or vendor, an independent poster, or unknown affiliation. Only the last two are candidates. Other employees cannot be identified: say so once. No handle: "no handle given", unknown affiliation.
3. Candidates, at most 10, most specific praise first, never by followers. For each: the excerpt exactly as returned, with "may continue" if cut (A: exactly 400 characters; B: ends in an ellipsis after a word; a link ending in one is not a cut); handle and display name; platform; date; link; engagement; author group; why it is worth a look; and "not verified: employer, whether a customer, permission to reuse".
4. Set aside, as counts, one example each: the company's own posts; partners and vendors; promotional and AI-written posts (by their tags in A, by reading in B); praise mainly of someone else; not praise when read.
5. End with: these are leads, and before reuse a person asks the author and waits for a yes in writing.

If you have run this before for {PRODUCT}, list only posts dated after that run. An earlier run is one in this conversation or your client's memory: do not search files.

Rules: Never complete, tidy, translate or join an excerpt, and add no quote from memory or the web. Nobody is a customer or a user unless the post says so. A display name that includes a company is not an employer. Never look an author up. With none, write "no candidates in the N posts read" and which reason removed the most.
